rv.q: Cho ("The Language Archive") is a confident writer, Gina is a gutsy character and Kim is a self-possessed performer, so the sensible, sympathetic teacher commands the stage for the first half of the play.
But the question remains: effective to what end?
Office Hour ultimately makes a defining decision that, for me, does little more than increase that fear’s dismal, daily weight.
But Office Hour doesn't earn its ending; it has nothing to teach.
Office Hour is both an important play and a compelling event in the theater.
Cho effectively calls for compassion and outreach from a society that commonly creates violent loners out of troubled children.
There's no denying the visceral intensity of this work.
The reality feels miserable enough, but the fantasies are lurid, and deathly!
As 'Office Hour' progresses, there are more resets that progressively build and become even more unsettling to watch and hear.
The net effect is a play in which two sets of concerns keep displacing each other.
Nowhere feels safe, not even the Public Theater, where this disturbing yet occasionally dull new play is having its New York debut.

But, given the almost 300 mass shootings in the United States so far this year alone, a play that uses gun violence in the opaque and overly clever way that “Office Hour” does will surely be ill-timed for some time to come.
Neel Keller directs some extraordinary scenes of imaginary violence that build to one extended fantasy sequence, which falls flat.
What’s left is a series of gunshots puncturing holes in a play.
Much of Office Hour is a two-hander filled with a tension that crackles in the air.
It’s a compelling thesis on the broken people and their broken attachments and ideas that sit on the edge of our conscious threatening us with violence and death.
These episodes contain lots of silence, more than pregnant pauses, that are off-putting and distracting which, in fact, director Neel Keller obviously didn’t count on.
Whether its approach is particularly helpful, though, is something else.
Unfortunately I thought the main effect of the play was to trivialize an important topic.
